newsitem.title: PERU: Peru arrests Ecuadorean soldiers on disputed border.
newsitem.headline: Peru arrests Ecuadorean soldiers on disputed border.

text.p: Peru said on Wednesday it had arrested seven Ecuadorean soldiers planting mines across a disputed border where the two Andean nations waged war in 1995.
Peru's military accused Ecuador of violating their peace agreement by sending troops into its territory, but Quito insisted its men were illegally detained on a routine patrol.

"This is a lamentable act and I hope it was an isolated case," said Gen. Daniel Mora, the Peruvian military's liaison with an international observer mission monitoring compliance of a provisional peace treaty that ended the month-long war.

"The incursion discovered yesterday, with a heavily armed Ecuadorean patrol laying mines six kilometres (four miles) inside our territory, constitutes a clear violation of the agreement," he told journalists in the northern city of Bagua.
The arrests came as negotiators from Lima and Quito began a second round of talks in the Brazilian capital of Brasilia on a permanent solution to the decades-old border dispute.

A Peruvian military statement said one sergeant, two corporals and four soldiers were detained with a haul that included four boxes containing 600 anti-personnel mines, German-made guns, infra-red binoculars, five rocket and grenade launchers, maps and cameras.

Gen. Eduardo Ortega, second-in-command of the border region, told reporters in Bagua that "according to the declarations from the (Ecuadorean) soldiers, they had orders from their command to mine the territory...they said this".

Ecuador's defence ministry issued a communique saying seven soldiers were illegally arrested while "carrying out normal activities and routine patrols" in the Paquisha Alto sector of the disputed frontier.
The arrested soldiers would be handed back "in the next few hours," the communique added. It also demanded a full report on the incident from Peru to lodge a diplomatic complaint.

Gen. Mora, however, said the soldiers would be handed over to Ecuadorean authorities in accordance with the peace agreement signed by the two countries and the Geneva Convention. "The soldiers will be turned over to the Ecuadorean authorities, probably tomorrow," Mora said.

Peruvian Congress President Victor Joy Way said the incident was "worrying...because it broke the commitment between the two nations and affects the peace talks that are underway...(it) disturbs the atmosphere."

"This action must have something to do with internal political problems in Ecuador," he added. "There is a referendum in the process, and some extreme militaristic and political groups are not in favour of peace."

The Ecuadorean soldiers were being held in Bagua, a city 845 miles (1,350 km) north of Lima from where Peru coordinated its military operations in 1995. That brief but bloody conflict left dozens dead and hundreds injured on both sides.

The talks in Brasilia centre on interpretation of a 1942 agreement signed in Rio de Janeiro. Argentina, Brazil, Chile and the United States are the guarantors of that accord and are represented on the mission overseeing the border dispute.
The head of Peru's armed forces, Gen. Nicolas de Bari Hermoza, flew Wednesday to the area where the Ecuadorean soldiers were being held.
